extracted.intended_audience: educated British public / political class (readers of a political pamphlet/essay)
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative political essay defending established institutions (church, monarchy, aristocracy, mixed government) and urging cautious, reverent reform rather than subversion. The text offers principles for justifying and preserving social/political order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: “We know, and what is better we feel inwardly, that religion is the basis of civil society, and the source of all good and of all comfort.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion should be regarded as fundamental to social order; abandoning it risks leaving a void that will be filled by ‘uncouth, pernicious, and degrading superstition.’ The text warns against invoking atheism to ‘explain’ or reform religious tenets and argues religion supplies moral instincts and consolations necessary for citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an established church integrated with the state
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are resolved to keep an established church... each in the degree it exists, and in no greater.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The established church is presented as inseparable from the constitution; it consecrates the state and imbues officeholders with moral purpose. The church should be publicly funded, stable, and intertwined with civic institutions to sustain public virtue and social cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a mixed constitution (church, monarchy, aristocracy, democracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are resolved to keep an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each in the degree it exists, and in no greater.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates keeping each element of the mixed constitution in its existing proportion rather than abolishing or exaggeratedly expanding any part. The balance preserves continuity, prevents rash experiments, and sustains ordered liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of the state by religion to promote virtue in rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: “This consecration is made, that all who administer in the government of men... should have high and worthy notions of their function and destination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A religious establishment elevates officeholders' sense of trust and accountability to a higher moral authority, discouraging pursuit of temporal gain and encouraging long-term, virtuous stewardship of public power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid calling in extreme or hostile principles to reform institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: “We shall never be such fools as to call in an enemy to the substance of any system to remove its corruptions... If our religious tenets should ever want a further elucidation, we shall not call on atheism to explain them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should not rely on radical or antithetical doctrines (e.g., atheism) to correct defects. Changes must come from compatible, measured sources rather than from forces that would destroy the system's foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should confirm attachment to church and constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our education is so formed as to confirm and fix this impression... our youth... three-fourths of those who go abroad with our young nobility and gentlemen are ecclesiastics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education—largely in ecclesiastical hands—should cultivate loyalty to established institutions. Clergy as tutors/companions help bind elite youth to church and state, creating lifelong connections between ruling classes and religious authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and continuity across generations (state as intergenerational partnership)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state should be treated as a long-term, intergenerational trust; policies and institutions ought not to be repeatedly overturned by passing fashions or transient majorities. Such continuity secures law, property, education, and civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisprudence and settled laws are essential to civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: “The science of jurisprudence... is the collected reason of ages... Of course, no certain laws... would keep the actions of men in a certain course.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining established legal frameworks and studied jurisprudence is necessary for stable property, predictable social expectations, effective education, and transmission of honor; undermining law leads to barbarism and social collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach reform cautiously; do not begin by subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: “To avoid therefore the evils of inconstancy and versatility... we have consecrated the state, that no man should approach to look into its defects or corruptions but with due caution; that he should never dream of beginning its reformation by its subversion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism and reform must be measured and reverent—treat the state's faults like the wounds of a father. Radical overthrow is condemned; repair should be incremental and respectful of institutional continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent popular will from becoming the sole standard of right
rubrics_metrics.description: “They ought to be persuaded that they are full as little entitled, and far less qualified, with safety to themselves, to use any arbitrary power whatsoever... they are not... to exercise an unnatural, inverted domination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit majoritarian absolutism; cultivate among the populace an understanding that their will is not the absolute moral standard. Political education and institutions should check arbitrary popular power to protect moral principle and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confer offices on persons of virtue and wisdom, not caprice
rubrics_metrics.description: “They will confer that power... on those only in whom they may discern that predominant proportion of active virtue and wisdom, taken together and fitted to the charge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments to public office should prioritize moral character and practical wisdom over transient popularity, selfish interest, or capricious choice; office is a ‘holy function’ requiring appropriate fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the clergy constitutionally independent of the state treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: “They certainly never have suffered, and never will suffer, the fixed estate of the church to be converted into a pension, to depend on the treasury... The people of England think that they have constitutional motives... against any project of turning their independent clergy into ecclesiastical pensioners of state.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church revenues must be secured and kept distinct from direct state control to prevent clerical dependence on politicians, which would threaten both liberty and religious integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public ceremonial and modest splendour strengthen national cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: “It will be performed... in buildings, in music, in decoration, in speech, in the dignity of persons... with modest splendour and unassuming state, with mild majesty and sober pomp.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public rites, ceremonies, and respectful display (funded as public ornament) reinforce collective identity and dignity, giving all citizens—especially the poor—a sense of belonging and shared esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church revenue should serve public charity but not be micromanaged
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is true, the whole church revenue is not always employed, and to every shilling, in charity — nor perhaps ought it; but something is generally so employed... It is better to cherish virtue and humanity, by leaving much to free will.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some church funds should aid the poor, not all revenue must be centrally directed to charity; preserving discretionary uses encourages virtue and voluntary beneficence rather than mechanistic political redistribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing religion to a tool to keep the vulgar obedient
rubrics_metrics.description: “If by their conduct... they seemed to regard the great ruling principle... as a mere invention to keep the vulgar in obedience, they apprehend that by such a conduct they would defeat the politic purpose they have in view.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious establishments must be sincere and convincingly practiced by leaders; hypocrisy (professing religion while living contemptuously of it) undercuts moral authority and the efficacy of religious institutions in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect clergy from lay contempt through adequate status
rubrics_metrics.description: “What must they think of that body of teachers, if they see it in no part above the establishment of their domestic servants?... Our provident constitution has therefore taken care that those who are to instruct... should neither incur their contempt, nor live upon their alms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clergy have sufficient social and economic standing to maintain influence and respect among the wealthy and powerful; forced poverty undermines their authority and the transmission of moral teaching.
